What does CSM2 Finance actually do?

We structure the transaction: technical scope, procurement content, contracts, risk allocation and debt structure aligned into one lender-facing package. We are not the EPC contractor and we are not the lender.
Turnkey delivery logic combined with financing structuring, so the project is developed as one bankable transaction architecture, not as a construction contract with a financing line attached later.
Does a project have to be fully developed?
No. A project does not need to be perfect at screening. It needs a credible route to close the gaps.
What do you need to screen a project?
Project location, sector, estimated investment size, development stage, expected procurement route and financing objective.
Are you tied to a technology or supplier?
No. Our role is technology-neutral and sponsor- and transaction-focused. Supplier origin is tested against ECA rules, not chosen in advance.
Do you stay involved after financial close?
We can. Many mandates stop when the loan documents are signed; we can continue into drawdown, documentation, contractor interfaces and compliance.

When is a project EPC+F-ready? Six questions before you approach a lender — CSM2 Finance
When is a project EPC+F-ready? Six questions before you approach a lender
A project does not need to be perfect at screening. It needs a credible route to close the gaps.
Lenders and ECAs test the same six things in every project, whatever the sector.
At screening, gaps are normal. Gaps without an owner are the problem.
Approach lenders when each open item has an owner, a deliverable and a date.

Projects tend to reach lenders at the wrong moment. Some arrive too early, as a concept with a price attached. Others arrive too late, with contracts signed and procurement fixed in a form that no export credit agency can support. In both cases the first meeting is spent discovering what is missing, and a first impression in a credit committee is hard to revise.

We use six questions to decide whether a project is ready for that meeting. They are the questions a lender, an ECA and their advisers will ask anyway. Answering them first, on the sponsor’s side of the table, turns the meeting from an examination into a negotiation.
Is the technical scope defined well enough to price and to diligence?

Capacity, design basis and scope of supply need to be fixed at a level the lenders’ technical adviser can test. A CAPEX figure that still moves with every design iteration undermines the model, the contract and the cover application built on it.
Who borrows, and what stands behind them?

Who borrows, who owns the asset, and what balance-sheet or sovereign support exists. The financing route follows the borrower: a ministry of finance, a state-owned company with a guarantee, a corporate and a project company each lead to a different structure.
A budget allocation, operating cash flow, a tariff, a power purchase or off-take agreement, an escrow arrangement. Lenders finance a repayment source. The asset is how that source is created.
Can the supply chain create eligible export content?
ECA support follows exports. The question is whether sourcing can generate enough eligible value for the intended agency without distorting the technical solution. We cover this in a separate note.
Are environmental, social, land and permitting risks on a credible path?

ECAs and development finance institutions apply environmental and social standards of their own. A missing impact assessment or an unresolved land question can stop a transaction that is sound in every other respect.
Can the contracts allocate risk on bankable terms?

Completion, performance, interfaces between packages and payment milestones each have to sit with a party able to carry them. A delivery model that leaves interface risk with the borrower is hard to finance as drafted.
The same six questions, at three points in time.

No project scores full marks at screening, and it does not need to. What separates a financeable project from a stalled one is whether each gap has a route to closure: a study commissioned, a guarantee under discussion, a sourcing plan being tested against agency rules.

We therefore look at each question in three states: where the project stands at screening, what the route to close looks like, and what must be true at financial close. The profile above is illustrative. The point it makes is general: the six areas do not mature at the same speed, and the slowest one sets the date of financial close.

The right moment is when every open item has an owner, a deliverable and a date, and when the answers are consistent with one another. A repayment source that assumes a sovereign guarantee, next to a borrower structure that assumes none, tells a lender more about the project than any presentation.
If that consistency is not there yet, the budget is better spent on closing gaps than on a roadshow.
This note sets out CSM2 Finance’s general approach. It is not legal or financial advice, and each transaction turns on its own facts.
ECA content is a structuring variable, not a procurement afterthought — CSM2 Finance
ECA content is a structuring variable, not a procurement afterthought
Where equipment and services come from decides which agencies can support a project, and for how much.
Export credit support is sized on the export contract, so sourcing decisions set the size of the facility.
Agencies apply different content rules. The lead agency and the sourcing plan have to be chosen together.
Fix the content strategy before the EPC package is locked, and write it into the contracts.

An export credit agency supports exports from its own country. That simple fact has a consequence that is often noticed late: the origin of goods and services is more than a procurement matter. It determines which agencies can take part, how large the supported facility can be, and on what terms.
For agencies that follow the OECD Arrangement on Officially Supported Export Credits, the general rules are these.
Maximum share of the export contract value that can receive official support
Minimum down payment by the buyer
Local costs that can be supported, as a share of the export contract value: 40% for Category I countries, 50% for Category II

Everything is measured against the export contract value. A project with a large, locally sourced civil works component and a modest imported equipment package may find that the supportable amount covers far less of total cost than the sponsor assumed. The reverse also holds: placing more eligible value inside the export contract can change the financing plan materially.

Content rules are set agency by agency. German export credit guarantees, for example, can include foreign content of up to 49% without special justification. UK Export Finance, in its 2019 consultation on foreign content, described a requirement of at least 20% UK content. Other agencies set their own thresholds and their own definitions of what counts.

Tenor is affected too. Since the 2023 revision of the Arrangement, the maximum repayment term is 15 years for most transactions and up to 22 years for certain climate-friendly projects. Which agency leads, and how the project is classified, shapes the repayment profile as well as the amount.
Sourcing is decided on price and technical preference alone, and the eligible content turns out to be too low for the intended agency.
Content is spread across several countries, so that no single agency has enough at stake to lead.
The EPC contract does not separate eligible and ineligible items, and every later drawdown becomes a negotiation.
Origin is assumed, not documented, and the evidence cannot be produced when the agency asks for it.

Treat content as one of the variables being solved for, alongside scope, price and schedule. In practice that means mapping realistic sourcing options against the rules of the candidate agencies before tender documents are issued; deciding which agency leads and whether others need to share cover; and writing the result into the contract structure, with a price breakdown that distinguishes export content, local costs and everything else.
The test is whether the supply chain can create eligible export value without distorting the technical solution.

The order matters. The technical solution comes first, because a project re-engineered around a financing rule tends to pay for it during operation. Between technically equivalent options, though, the one that can be financed is the better one.
Down payment, maximum official support and local costs: Norton Rose Fulbright, Recent amendments to the OECD allowing ECA to offer 95% coverage on export contracts, January 2024.

Repayment terms after the 2023 revision: DLA Piper, OECD publishes revised version of Arrangement on Officially Supported Export Credits, 1 August 2023; Mayer Brown, OECD Arrangement on Officially Supported Export Credits, 8 August 2023.
German foreign content: Export Credit Guarantees of the Federal Republic of Germany, fact sheet on foreign content, May 2021.
UK content: UK Export Finance, Foreign Content Policy consultation document, 2019.

Financial close is not the finish line — CSM2 Finance
Financial close is not the finish line
Signing the finance documents starts a second project: getting the facility drawn, on time, against documents that withstand scrutiny.
A signed facility is a right to borrow, subject to conditions. It is not cash.
Each drawdown is checked against the contract, the cover and the facility agreement.
The disbursement procedure should be designed before signing, with the contractor in the room.

Financial close is celebrated as the end of a long process, and for the people who negotiated the term sheet it is. For the project it is the point at which the financing has to start working. Between signing and the last disbursement lie conditions precedent, a long series of drawdown requests and a reporting calendar that runs for the life of the loan.

In an ECA-backed facility each disbursement is tied to evidence: that goods were shipped or work performed, that the amount claimed is eligible, and that the borrower remains in compliance. The checks are not difficult. They are unforgiving of inconsistency.
Invoices that do not follow the price breakdown in the contract.
Certificates of origin or shipping documents that are missing, late or issued by the wrong party.
Local-cost claims that exceed the supported limit.
Milestone certificates that do not match the payment schedule in the facility agreement.
Variations to scope that change the eligible content without the lenders being told.
Conditions precedent treated as a one-off exercise when several are continuing obligations.

Each of these delays payment to the contractor. A contractor who is not paid slows down, and a delayed project runs up against the availability period of the facility. Problems in the back office reach the construction site quickly.
A facility that cannot be drawn is not financing.
Most of this can be prevented at the structuring stage, while the documents are still in draft.
Agree the disbursement procedure with the lenders, the agency and the contractor, and test it against a sample invoice.
Align the contract price breakdown with the categories the facility recognises: export content, local costs and ineligible items.
Decide who prepares, who checks and who signs each document in a drawdown file.
Build one tracker for conditions precedent, covenants and reporting dates, and give it an owner.
Define how variations will be assessed for their effect on eligibility before they are approved.
None of this is sophisticated. It is the difference between a financing structure that exists on paper and one that pays the contractor on the day the contract says it should.
